$comment: Family stories — narrative pieces that capture oral history, research breakthroughs, and the human texture behind the names and dates in family.json. Listed newest-first; the stories.html page renders all entries inline so each story is deep-linkable via #story-{id}.

stories.title: Ita's move to Drimnagh — and the return to Goldenbridge
stories.summary: When Ita Greene married John Donnelly in 1958 they did what young Dublin couples in that decade did — they bought their own home in the nearby suburb of Drimnagh. But when Ita's mother Bridget became unwell in the 1960s, they brought their young family back to 38 Goldenbridge Avenue to care for her until her death in August 1970.
stories.body:
Ita Donnelly grew up at 38 Goldenbridge Avenue, Inchicore — a Dublin Corporation social-housing terrace built in the 1930s as part of the city's ambitious plan to move families out of inner-city tenements into purpose-built suburban homes. Her parents Thomas Greene (a warehouse porter) and Bridget Clarke (a cook from Co. Meath) had moved there together in the early-to-mid 1930s after their marriage at Holy Cross Church, Dundrum in 1922.

When Ita married John Donnelly around 1958, the couple set up their own home in Drimnagh — the Dublin 12 suburb directly beside Inchicore and Goldenbridge. The journey between the two houses was a short bus ride, but for a young couple in late-1950s Ireland it was the proper first step of married life: their own front door, their own address, their own household.

That changed when Bridget became unwell. By the 1960s John and Ita had moved their growing family — four children eventually: Ann, John Jr, Sheila, and Ger — back into 38 Goldenbridge Avenue so that Bridget could be cared for at home rather than in hospital. It was a generational continuity that anyone with Irish family ties will recognise: the youngest daughter returns to the family home to mind her mother through her final years.

Bridget Clarke died on 9 August 1970 at the Adelaide Hospital, Dublin, age 78. Her death was registered by her son Brendan. Ita continued to live, work, and raise her family in Inchicore. She passed away peacefully on 6 December 2025 at Kiltipper Woods Care Centre, age 91, surrounded by her family. Her funeral Mass was held at St. Michael's Church, Inchicore — the same parish where she had been baptised, married, and lived her entire adult life.

Why this story is in the site: Civil registers can tell us when Bridget died and where Ita lived, but they cannot tell us why a young couple decided to leave their own home in Drimnagh and move back into a busy multi-generational household in Inchicore. That kind of knowledge only survives in living memory. Thank you to Claire Garrigan (née Donnelly) — Ita's granddaughter, daughter of Ann — for sharing this on 6 June 2026. It has been folded into the family.json record for Ita and her parents, with this story preserving the full context.
relatedSources: Claire Garrigan (née Donnelly) family contribution, 6 June 2026 (Phase 12 oral history, relayed via Mark Garrigan)
Civil death register: Bridget Greene née Clarke, 9 August 1970, Dublin, age 78 (registered by Brendan Greene)
RIP.ie death notice: Ita Donnelly née Greene, 6 December 2025

stories.title: Married during the occupation — Elizabeth Bessie Greene's Jersey wedding, 13 September 1941
stories.summary: On 13 September 1941, fourteen months into the German occupation of the Channel Islands, Elizabeth Bessie Greene married Alfred Bower Harris at the Catholic church of St Mary and St Peter, Vauxhall, Jersey. A primary-source marriage certificate held in the family papers fixes the date, the place, and the witnesses. A year later both were deported to the Biberach internment camp in southern Germany, where Elizabeth worked as a nurse under Dr. A.W.H. Donaldson until liberation in May 1945.
stories.body:
Of all the stories on this site, Elizabeth Bessie Greene's might be the most dramatic. The daughter of Thomas Christopher Greene (his first wife Elizabeth Farrell's child), born in Dublin around 1907, she had moved to Jersey by the late 1930s and was working as a nurse in the parish of St. Saviour's.

On 30 June 1940 the German army landed unopposed on Jersey — the only piece of British soil that Nazi Germany occupied during World War II. The Channel Islands had been militarily indefensible after the fall of France and the British government had withdrawn forces and offered evacuation. About 30,000 people stayed.

Fourteen months into the occupation, on 13 September 1941, Elizabeth Bessie Greene married Alfred Bower Harris, a 28-year-old English-born printer from Bretforton, Worcestershire, who was also living in St. Saviour's. The marriage was solemnised at the Church of St Mary and St Peter, Vauxhall in St. Helier — a Catholic church just a short walk from the harbour where German naval patrols ran daily. The marriage certificate, held in the family papers and recovered as a primary source in April 2026, records:

Extract from the Register of Marriages, Parish of St. Helier, Island of Jersey, Page 97, 1941.

Alfred Bower Harris, 28, Bachelor, Printer, of St. Saviour's, son of Charles Edward Harris (deceased).

Elizabeth Bessie Greene, 34, Spinster, Nurse, of St. Saviour's, daughter of Thomas Greene (Retired).

By certificate of the Superintendent Registrar. Officiant: Richard T. Arnett. Witnesses: F.C. Colligny and C.M. Colligny. Deputy Registrar: W.A. de la Perrelle.

One detail from that certificate is its own small piece of evidence: Thomas Greene is recorded as "Retired". That places him alive in September 1941 and no longer working — consistent with his later death certificate (1951, Goldenbridge Avenue, Dublin, age 81, Warehouse Porter at the end).

A year after the wedding the Germans, in retaliation for Britain's deportation of German nationals from occupied Iran, ordered the deportation of all English-born civilians and their families from the Channel Islands. Around 2,300 people were rounded up between September 1942 and February 1943. Elizabeth and Alfred — she Irish-born, he English-born — were caught in that net. They were sent to Biberach an der Riß in southern Germany, to Ilag V-B ("Internment Camp Detainees, Camp 5-B"), where Channel Islanders were held for the rest of the war.

At Biberach, Elizabeth's training as a nurse mattered. A letter held in the family papers, dated 21 May 1945 — four weeks after French forces liberated the camp — was written by Dr. A.W.H. Donaldson, M.B., D.P.H., the camp's senior medical officer. It records that Elizabeth had worked for two years at the Men's Hospital under his supervision. In a camp of two thousand people, with German rations and limited medical supplies, nurses kept other people alive.

Open research: the Arolsen Archives (formerly the International Tracing Service) holds the surviving Nazi-era records of detainees and survivors including civilian internees at Biberach. Several online search variants for "Elizabeth Harris", "Bessie Harris", and "Alfred Harris" have not yet returned a confirmed hit — but Arolsen's web index is incomplete and the surest path forward is a free inquiry to the archives staff directly (linked from their main search page). Roger E. Harris's book Islanders Deported contains the full Biberach internee list and is another high-confidence lookup.

What happened to Elizabeth and Alfred after 1945 — when and where they died, whether they had children, whether they returned to Jersey or to Dublin or to England — is also still open in the research. Both their death records are unconfirmed. If any reader has documents, photographs, or memories that touch on Elizabeth Bessie Greene/Harris, please share them.
relatedSources: MARRIAGE CERTIFICATE (PRIMARY SOURCE): Extract from the Register of Marriages, Parish of St. Helier, Jersey, Page 97, 1941 — Alfred Bower Harris × Elizabeth Bessie Greene, 13 September 1941 (held in family papers)
Letter of recommendation from Dr. A.W.H. Donaldson, M.B., D.P.H., Biberach Internment Camp, 21 May 1945
Arolsen Archives online search (collections.arolsen-archives.org) — multiple name variants attempted; no confirmed hit, search remains open

stories.title: Thomas at Switzers — a Dublin tenement Census, 2 April 1926
stories.summary: The 1926 Census places Thomas Christopher Greene at York Street, Dublin, age 55 years 9 months, working as Shop Porter for Switzers & Co. Drapers — the prestigious Grafton Street department store. The household: Thomas, his second wife Bridget Clarke, three young sons, and his adult stepson Patrick from the first marriage. All in two rooms.
stories.body:
By the time the 1926 Census enumerator knocked on the door of the family's rooms at York Street, Dublin, Thomas Christopher Greene had survived the loss of his first wife Elizabeth Farrell, remarried Bridget Clarke at Holy Cross Church in Dundrum (June 1922), and started a second family. He was 55 years and 9 months old — the unusually precise age recorded "to the month" by the 1926 Census, which gives us a birth around July 1870.

The household form lists him as Head of family, Shop Porter, employer Switzers & Co. Drapers. Switzers was one of Dublin's most prestigious retail institutions — a Grafton Street department store founded in 1838 that would later, in 1995, be absorbed into Brown Thomas. To walk from York Street to Grafton Street is about ten minutes through some of the most Georgian streets in Europe — past the Royal College of Surgeons, across St Stephen's Green, and on to Grafton Street. Thomas would have made that walk every working morning.

Bridget, his second wife, is recorded as Head's Wife, age 34 years 4 months, Home Duties, born Meath/Duleek. The three boys were Thomas Jr (later "Thomas Greene II", who would emigrate to New Zealand and marry a Samoan woman), Brendan, and John — the first wave of what would become a four-child family with the addition of Ita a few years later.

Also in the household was Patrick Greene, age 23, a stepson — Thomas's child from the first marriage with Elizabeth Farrell. He shared a roof with his step-siblings and step-mother in what was, by London or modern Dublin standards, a tiny apartment: two rooms total. This was Dublin tenement life in the 1920s, before the Corporation's housing programme would replace much of the inner-city with the suburban estates of the 1930s.

The Greenes themselves benefited from that programme in the early-to-mid 1930s, when they moved out to 38 Goldenbridge Avenue, Inchicore — the corporation-built home that would anchor the family for the next 90 years, where Thomas himself would die in December 1951, where Bridget would care for the family until her death in 1970, and where Ita would return in the 1960s to care for her mother and remain for the rest of her life.

A small detail worth noting: the 1926 Census is the most recent Irish census whose detail-level forms have been released to the public (April 2026 release, 100-year embargo). For families like the Greenes whose 20th-century lives spanned tenement Dublin, the Corporation housing boom, and the post-war suburban move, the 1926 Census is often the first fully detailed look at a household between the 1911 Census and the post-1950 civil register evidence.
relatedSources: 1926 Census of Ireland (released April 2026): York Street, Dublin household — Thomas Greene, Head, age 55y 9m, Shop Porter, Switzers & Co. Drapers; Bridget Greene, Wife, age 34y 4m, Home Duties, born Meath/Duleek; sons Thomas, Brendan, John; stepson Patrick (age 23)
IrishGenealogy.ie civil marriage register cima-1271568 — Thomas Greene × Bridget Clarke, 20 June 1922, Holy Cross, Dundrum
Civil death register: Thomas Christopher Greene, 6 December 1951, 38 Goldenbridge Avenue, Inchicore, age 81 (cause: carcinoma of stomach, cachexia, cardiac failure; registered by his son John Greene)

stories.title: Bridget Clarke — a cook in a Dublin magistrate's house
stories.summary: Born in a labourer's cottage in Mullaghfin, Co. Meath in December 1891, Bridget Clarke had moved to Dublin by her late teens. The 1911 Census places her at age 19 working as Cook (Domestic) in the household of Joseph Dollard — Justice of the Peace and Printer-Master. By 1922 she was Housekeeper at Drummartin House, Dundrum, where she would marry Thomas Greene at Holy Cross church.
stories.body:
In 1891 the village of Mullaghfin, Duleek, Co. Meath was a small farming community of cottages, fields, and stone-built labourers' homes. On 2 December 1891, Bridget Clarke was born there, daughter of Pat Clark (labourer) and Catherine née Clinton. Her father registered the birth on 26 December.

By 1901 Bridget was nine years old and Catherine was a widow with six children to support. The 1901 Census records the household at House 3, Mullaghfin: Catherine (40, widow, General Labourer) and her children Rose (23), Patrick (18), Mary (12), Jane (10), Bridget (9), and Agnes (5). Six children in a labourer's cottage with no man's wage coming in is a hard arithmetic.

Within ten years Bridget had crossed the country to Dublin. The 1911 Census — Form A, Form B No. 142, enumerated 2 April 1911 by Robert J. Holmes — places her at age 19, working as Cook (Domestic) in the household of Joseph Dollard, recorded as Justice of the Peace and Printer-Master. To hold the senior kitchen role at nineteen was a remarkable rise from a labourer's cottage in Mullaghfin. It also says something about Bridget herself — by then she could read and write, she was running a kitchen for a magistrate's family, and she had figured out how to leave the home county and build a position in Dublin's middle-class service economy.

Eleven years on, the 1922 marriage register at Holy Cross Church, Dundrum records her as Housekeeper at Drummartin House, Dundrum — the next step up from cook, with responsibility for the whole household, not just the kitchen. Drummartin House and Holy Cross church sit a short walk from each other in the leafy south Dublin suburb. On 20 June 1922 she married Thomas Greene there — he a widower, warehouseman from the city; she the housekeeper from Drummartin House.

The marriage register names her father as Patrick Clarke, occupation "Farmer" — slightly different from her 1891 birth register's "Labourer". The shift may reflect later land-holding by her father, or simply how a confident 30-year-old woman remembered and described him to the registrar.

Why this story is in the site: family oral history had remembered Bridget as a cook in service in Dublin before her marriage to Thomas — but the family did not know which household. The original 1911 Census form filled in the picture: a specific employer, a specific street, a specific job title. Pair that with the 1922 register's "Housekeeper at Drummartin House, Dundrum" and you have a young Co. Meath woman's first decade in Dublin laid out in two documents.
relatedSources: 1911 Census Form A, Form B No. 142 — Joseph Dollard household, Dublin: Bridget Clarke, age 19, Cook (Domestic)
IrishGenealogy.ie civil marriage register cima-1271568 — Thomas Greene × Bridget Clarke, 20 June 1922, Holy Cross, Dundrum (her recorded address: Drummartin House, Dundrum)
IrishGenealogy.ie civil birth register civbi-9688899 — Bridget Clarke, born 2 December 1891 Mullaghfin, Duleek, parents Pat Clark + Catherine née Clinton

stories.title: A village wedding in February 1868 — and a new generation joins the tree
stories.summary: Cross-checking five Irish civil register images at the same time, the Phase 18 research batch landed the strongest evidence yet for Thomas Christopher Greene's father: William Green, a Bachelor Labourer of Lower Forest near Mountmellick, who married Eliza Woods on 25 February 1868. Most importantly, the register names William's own father — Thomas Green, a farmer — a previously unknown ancestor.
stories.body:
For most of the year we had a name and not much else. The 1922 marriage register at Holy Cross, Dundrum had told us in April 2026 that Thomas Christopher Greene's father was named William Greene, occupation "Traveller" (almost certainly meaning a commercial traveller — a respectable late-Victorian travelling salesman who went from town to town selling goods on commission). But which William? The Portarlington area had several Williams at the right time: William Greene of Imacrannagh (farmer with a large family), William Greene of Shanderry (labourer, with a 1901 census note that his husband was "working in Dublin"), and assorted other Williams in the wider Co. Laois countryside.

Phase 18 of the research — completed in June 2026 — pulled five candidate civil register images from IrishGenealogy.ie to try to disambiguate. The breakthrough came from one record: cima-2999201, an 1868 marriage register from Mountmellick.

The register reads:

25 February 1868. Roman Catholic Chapel of Mountmellick, Union of Mountmellick, Queens County.

William Green, full age, Bachelor, Labourer, of Lower Forest. Father: Thomas Green, Farmer.

Eliza Woods, full age, Spinster, of The Borneass. Father: John Woods, Farmer.

The age, location, and timing all fit. "Full age" in the 1868 register meant 21 or over — so William was born by 1847. The two later death candidates from Mountmellick (1909 William age 66; 1910 William age 67) both point to a birth year around 1843. Lower Forest is a townland next to Mountmellick, about 12 miles north of Portarlington where Thomas Christopher Greene was baptised around July 1870. A young couple newly married in February 1868 having their first son in mid-1870 is exactly what the chronology requires.

And — if this William Green is our William — then the tree gains a new generation. Thomas Green Snr, a farmer of Lower Forest in Queens County, would be Claire Garrigan's great-great-great-grandfather (her line: Claire → Ann → Ita → Thomas Christopher Greene Jnr → William Greene → Thomas Green Snr). The naming pattern is exactly what Irish Roman Catholic tradition would predict: a man's first son is named for his own father, and our Thomas Christopher Greene Jnr is named just that.

The remaining piece of evidence we need is the actual baptism record of Thomas Greene Jnr. The Phase 18 batch captured the NLI Portarlington Catholic parish register pages 142–145 (April 1870 to January 1871) at high resolution, but the Greene baptism entry has not yet been located there. The next thread — Phase 19, dispatched the same day — is checking the Mountmellick Catholic parish register, which is the geographically natural baptism location for a family living at Lower Forest. If that register names parents William Greene and Eliza Woods, the candidate becomes a confirmed ancestor and the new generation lands in the tree.

Research note: Three of the other four register images in the Phase 18 batch turned out to be IrishGenealogy.ie image-link mismatches — the transcription panel for a given record was correct (the indexed civil entry was who it claimed to be) but the linked register PDF showed a different person from the same volume. The pattern is now documented in research-results/RESEARCH_ROADMAP.md under "Known research-tooling constraints". It does not invalidate any of the transcribed evidence; it just means that for those four records the register image needs to be re-located by paging adjacent files, or a GRO certified copy needs to be ordered.
relatedSources: IrishGenealogy.ie civil marriage register cima-2999201 — William Green × Eliza Woods, 25 February 1868, Mountmellick (register image transcribed Phase 18)
IrishGenealogy.ie civil marriage register cima-1271568 — Thomas Greene × Bridget Clarke, 20 June 1922, Dundrum (the original record that named William as Thomas's father)

stories.title: From "née unknown" to Elizabeth Farrell — finding Thomas's first wife
stories.summary: For most of the project, Thomas Christopher Greene's first wife Elizabeth was a name with no surname — "née unknown" — alongside the few facts we could pull from the 1901 and 1911 censuses. The Phase 15 research breakthrough on 6 June 2026 pulled her actual marriage register from IrishGenealogy.ie and confirmed: she was Elizabeth Farrell, daughter of Patrick Farrell.
stories.body:
Three Greene children, three census forms, and several years of family research had all referred to Thomas's first wife as just Elizabeth. The 1911 census recorded her as Elizabeth Greene, wife of Thomas, age 41, born Co. Dublin, married 12 years with three children born and three living — but the census could not tell us her maiden name. An earlier index lookup had wrongly pointed us at Dublin South Vol. 2, Page 593 for the marriage; the register did not match.

Phase 15 of the research went back to IrishGenealogy.ie and ran the search again, this time across both Dublin North and Dublin South registration districts for any Thomas Greene marriage 1898–1900. The hit came from Dublin North, entry 72, record cima-2399599:

30 July 1899. Roman Catholic Chapel of Fairview, in the Registrar's District of Dublin North.

Thomas Greene, Bachelor, Labourer, of Henry Street, Clonliffe. Father: William Greene.

Elizabeth Farrell, Spinster, of Mayfield, Clonliffe. Father: Patrick Farrell.

Witnesses: Maurice F. Murphy and Agnes Murphy. Officiant: Bernard Reynolds.

Elizabeth's maiden name is Farrell. Her father was Patrick Farrell. The Fairview chapel is just north of the Royal Canal in inner Dublin, and both Mayfield and Henry Street were small streets in the Clonliffe / Drumcondra parish area — a handful of minutes' walk between the bride's and groom's addresses. The witnesses, Maurice and Agnes Murphy, were likely a married couple acting as the formal witnesses required by the Roman Catholic marriage rite.

The earlier "Dublin South Vol. 2 Page 593" index reference is now formally corrected in the family.json record — that index pointer was wrong. The actual register is Dublin North.

One question is still open: Elizabeth's death. She was alive at the April 1911 census but had died by the time Thomas married Bridget Clarke at Holy Cross, Dundrum on 20 June 1922. The candidate death record cide-5487276 (Elizabeth Green, Dublin South, age 43, 1916) is plausible but needs the register image to confirm. The age 43 in 1916 would imply Elizabeth was born around 1873 — close enough to the 1911 census age 41 (born ~1870) that the rounding is normal for the era.

Why this matters: with the Farrell name confirmed, the half-siblings Patrick Greene (b.1903) and Elizabeth "Bessie" Greene (later Mrs Alfred Harris of Jersey and Biberach) now have a fully named maternal line — Elizabeth Farrell, daughter of Patrick Farrell. The Farrell line itself is the next thing to push back, starting with Elizabeth's own birth in Dublin around 1870.
relatedSources: IrishGenealogy.ie civil marriage register cima-2399599 — Thomas Greene × Elizabeth Farrell, 30 July 1899, Fairview, Dublin North RD entry 72
1911 Census Form B No. 1842 — Clonliffe Avenue, Mountjoy: Elizabeth Greene age 41, 12 years married, 3 born / 3 living
